chapter.title: Face in, breath out

cards.body: Nobody holds their breath in bed, so why does almost everyone do it the moment their face touches water? Treat the water like a pillow. With your face in, you sigh into it the way you'd sigh into a pillow at night. **Breathe out into the water, breathe in above it**, and putting your face in stops being scary.
cards.simpler: Nobody holds their breath in bed. Yet almost everyone holds it the moment their face touches water. Think of the water as a pillow. With your face in, you can sigh into it, like sighing into a pillow at night. **Breathe out into the water, breathe in above it.** Once you do that, putting your face in stops being scary.

cards.prompt: Priya, 34, is standing in chest-deep water. She's about to put her face in for the first time. Which plan gets her through 3 seconds calmly?

options.text: Gulp the biggest breath she can and clamp it in
Let a slow stream of bubbles out through her nose and mouth
Pinch her nose and squeeze her eyes shut

whyNot.a: That's holding against the water, not breathing with it: a clamped breath makes her tense, and it leaves both breaths for one rushed second at the surface.
whyNot.c: That's bracing for a fall, not sighing into a pillow: breathing out through your nose keeps the water out by itself, so you don't need your fingers.

cards.reteach: In bed you don't hold your breath. You breathe out and let go. The water works the same way: your out-breath goes into the water as bubbles, and your in-breath happens after you lift your face.

cards.title: Why holding your breath backfires
cards.body:
Clamping a breath in usually makes you tense: shoulders up, jaw tight, counting down until it's over. And it saves both jobs for the surface, so you have to puff out and suck in during one rushed second. That rushed second is how people end up swallowing water.

Breathing out through your nose also keeps water out. While air is pushing out, water can't push in, the same way nothing climbs up a straw while you blow into it.

It also leaves only one job for when you come up. **Out happens underwater, in happens above.** Lift your face, take one breath through your mouth, and that's it.
cards.simpler: Holding your breath usually makes you tense. It also saves both jobs for the surface, so you have to breathe out and in during one rushed second. That's how people swallow water. Breathing out through your nose also keeps water out, the same way nothing climbs up a straw while you blow into it. **Out happens underwater, in happens above.** Lift your face, take one breath through your mouth, and that's it.

cards.title: Tom at the shallow end
cards.body: Tom, 41, stands chest-deep at the shallow end on a Tuesday evening, one hand on the wall. He puts his face in with his eyes open and hums *mmmm* for a slow count of 3. Bubbles fizz past his cheeks. He lifts until his mouth is clear, takes one breath in, and goes down again. By round 6 he notices he has stopped wiping his eyes between goes. **Breathing out was what calmed him down, not breathing in.** The lifeguard never looked up once, which is the best review a beginner can get.
cards.simpler: Tom is 41. On a Tuesday evening he stands chest-deep at the shallow end, one hand on the wall. He puts his face in with his eyes open and hums for a slow count of 3. Bubbles fizz past his cheeks. He lifts until his mouth is clear, takes one breath in, and goes down again. By round 6 he has stopped wiping his eyes. **Breathing out was what calmed him, not breathing in.** The lifeguard never looked up.

cards.prompt: Marco, 52, holds his breath with his face in for 3 seconds. When he lifts, he tries to puff out and suck in during one quick second, and he swallows a mouthful of pool. What should he change?

options.text: Stay under longer so he's more ready to breathe
Lift his whole chest out of the water to give himself more time
Breathe out underwater, so above the water he only breathes in

whyNot.a: That's more holding, not less: the longer he holds, the tenser he gets, and the breath out is still waiting for him at the surface.
whyNot.b: That's a bigger lift, not a better breath: the breath out still gets crammed into the same rushed second.

cards.reteach: Give each place one job. Underwater is for breathing out, slowly, as bubbles. Above the water is for one breath in. If the breath out is already done, coming up is easy.

cards.title: Eyes open, long out, short in
cards.body:
Open your eyes under there. Pool water can sting a little, and goggles are fine. What you get back is the floor tiles, the black line and your own toes. The water stops being a dark unknown and becomes a room you can see.

Then comes the rhythm. On land, at rest, your breath out is usually a little longer than your breath in. In the water you stretch that much further: **a long, slow breath out through your nose and mouth, then a short one in through your mouth.** About 3 seconds of bubbles, then one quick breath with your chin just above the surface.
cards.simpler: Keep your eyes open underwater. Pool water may sting a little, so goggles are fine. Seeing the tiles, the black line and your toes turns the water into a room you can see. On land, your breath out is usually a little longer than your breath in. In water you stretch that much further: **a long, slow breath out through your nose and mouth, then a short one in through your mouth.** Blow bubbles for about 3 seconds, then take one quick breath, chin just above the water.

cards.body: Ana knows she should breathe out, so the moment her face goes in she blows one huge whoosh. The bubbles boil for a second and then stop. She spends the last 2 seconds empty and tense, then comes up gasping. Here's how to spot it: **if the bubbles stop before you lift, you blew too hard.** Aim for a steady stream, like a slow leak from a bike tyre.
cards.simpler: Ana knows she should breathe out. So the moment her face goes in, she blows one huge whoosh. The bubbles boil for a second, then stop. She spends the last 2 seconds empty and tense, and comes up gasping. Here's the sign to watch for: **if the bubbles stop before you lift, you blew too hard.** Aim for a steady stream instead, like a slow leak from a bike tyre.

cards.prompt: A friend asks how to breathe with your face in the water. Which one-liner do you give them?

options.text: Big breath, hold it, blow it all out when you come up
Out slowly underwater, one breath in above
Blow everything out hard the second your face goes in

whyNot.a: That's the habit from land, not from water: holding makes you tense, and it leaves two jobs for the surface.
whyNot.c: That's the right direction at the wrong speed: a hard whoosh empties you in a second and leaves you underwater with nothing left.

cards.reteach: Think of a slow leak, not a burst. The bubbles should keep coming for the whole 3 seconds you're under and stop only as you lift. Then the only job at the surface is breathing in.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Put your face in with your eyes open and let a slow stream of bubbles out through your nose and mouth for about 3 seconds. Lift, take one breath in, and go again: **the water gets your breath out, the air gets your breath in**.
cards.simpler: Put your face in with your eyes open. Let a slow stream of bubbles out through your nose and mouth for about 3 seconds. Then lift, take one breath in, and go again. **The water gets your breath out, the air gets your breath in.**

cards.body:
Tonight, fill a bowl at the kitchen sink. Put your face in and hum bubbles out through your nose and mouth for 3 seconds. Lift and take one breath in. Do 10, with your eyes open if you can.

Tomorrow: lying back on the water, and why your lungs work like a mattress.
cards.simpler: Tonight, fill a bowl with water at the kitchen sink. Put your face in and **hum bubbles out through your nose and mouth for 3 seconds**. Lift your face and take one breath in. Do this 10 times, with your eyes open if you can. Tomorrow you'll learn about lying back on the water, and why your lungs work like a mattress.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now put your face in the water with your eyes open, breathe out for 3 seconds, and lift for one calm breath in, 10 times in a row.

dubious_claims: A held breath brings on the urge to breathe sooner than slowly breathing out does. With full lungs you can usually hold longer, so this is likely backwards.
'On land, breathing in and breathing out take about the same time.' At rest, breathing out is usually longer than breathing in, about 1 to 2.
Card 1's 'the water is the bed you lie on' doesn't fit a learner standing chest-deep, and floating is tomorrow's topic. It's a mixed metaphor, not a false fact, but it muddles the hook.
repairedFrom.why: The chapter's main 'why' (holding your breath makes the urge to breathe come sooner) is shaky body science: holding a full breath usually lets you stay under longer than breathing out does, so a careful reader may stop trusting the rest.
repairedFrom.fix: Swap the carbon dioxide paragraph for the real reason: a held breath makes you tense, and it forces you to breathe out and in during one rushed second at the surface, which is how Marco swallows water. Then move the 'Tomorrow: lungs work like a mattress' line onto the final try card so the chapter actually ends on it.
